  • Property is reassessed every 3 years, and the assessment increase is phased in equally over three years. (SDAT: Questions and Answers About Real Property Assessments; source)

Who sets and collects property tax in Maryland?

The state values the property, and local governments turn that value into a bill. SDAT assesses real property, certifies the assessments to counties and municipalities, and those governments apply their own rates.

The scale is large. SDAT's homeowner guide counts more than 2.3 million real property accounts across 23 counties, Baltimore City and 155 incorporated municipalities. Each state, county and municipal government sets its own rate, and the state does not cap rates. When a proposed rate is higher than the current one, the governing body must advertise it and hold a public hearing.

For a seller, this means two bills can land on one address: a county bill and a town or city bill.

What are typical Maryland property tax rates?

The State's real property rate is $0.112 per $100 of assessed value, and county rates differ widely on top of it. The table below comes from SDAT's published 2022-2023 rate sheet, so treat the county figures as a snapshot and check the current year with the county.

JurisdictionCounty real property rate per $100 (FY 2022-23)
Baltimore City2.2480
Baltimore County1.1000

Montgomery0.6940

A bill equals the assessment times the jurisdiction's rate, so a house in Baltimore City and an identical one in Montgomery County can carry very different taxes. Municipal governments set their own rates as well.

How often are Maryland homes reassessed?

Every property is reassessed once every three years, and each county is split into three regions so about one-third of its accounts are reviewed each year. Owners hear about a change in late December, when SDAT mails an assessment notice showing old and new market values with an appeal form.

Increases are phased in evenly over three years. SDAT's example has a value rising from $100,000 to $130,000 and taxed at $110,000, then $120,000, then $130,000. A decrease takes effect right away.

The 2026 cycle covered Group 2. The Maryland Association of Counties reported SDAT's figures as a 12.7% overall increase in assessed value, with residential up an average of 13.2% and commercial up 11%. That compares with 20.1% in the 2025 cycle and 23.4% in 2023. Those figures describe a statewide group, so your own notice is the number that counts.

When is Maryland property tax due?

The tax is due July 1 and can be paid without interest through September 30. After September 30 it is in arrears, according to Tax-Property § 10-102.

  • Bills go out each July or August for the fiscal year that starts July 1.
  • Counties and municipalities must offer a semiannual schedule for owner-occupied principal residences. The first installment is due July 1 and payable without interest through September 30, and the second is due December 1 and payable without interest through December 31.
  • The second installment can be prepaid through September 30 with no service charge.
  • Otherwise a service charge of no more than 1.5% of the second installment applies, plus capped administrative costs.

Interest after the overdue date is set locally. SDAT's tax sale page cites 1% per month in Anne Arundel County and 1.5% per month in Allegany County, so look at your own county's rule.

How do you appeal a Maryland assessment?

You start with the local assessment office, and you have 45 days from the date on the notice. The appeal can go through four levels, each with its own clock.

LevelDeadlineWho decides
Supervisor's level45 days from the notice dateAn assessor designated by the Supervisor of Assessments
Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board30 days from the final noticeLocal residents appointed by the Governor
Maryland Tax Court30 days from the board's orderAn independent body, in-person hearing
Circuit CourtFurther appealReviews the record for legal error

There is no filing fee at the board or Tax Court. SDAT tries to finish reassessment appeals by June 1, and the Supervisor's hearing is informal and usually about 15 minutes.

What evidence helps in an assessment appeal?

Evidence that speaks to market value works, and complaints about the tax bill do not. SDAT advises owners to explain why the Total New Market Value does not reflect market value, point out errors on the property worksheet such as a wrong bathroom or fireplace count, and bring comparable sales.

SDAT says to leave out past values, percentage increases, metropolitan cost arguments, tax bill amounts, and services received or not received. At the Tax Court, any outside properties you plan to cite must be listed at least 10 days in advance with sale date and price or assessment details.

Buyers have a separate path. If a property transfers between January 1 and June 30, the new owner can file a Petition for Review within 60 days of the transfer, once the deed is recorded in the land records. Owners can also file a petition for review by the first working day after January 1 in the two years when the property is not being reassessed, if they believe value has fallen.

Which tax credits and deferrals can lower a Maryland bill?

The main programs are the Homestead Tax Credit, the income-based Homeowners' Tax Credit and a deferral for older owners. SDAT's guide describes each.

  • Homestead Tax Credit: applies when a principal residence's taxable assessment rises more than the local cap, which is 10% or lower. One application establishes eligibility.
  • Homeowners' Tax Credit: an income-based sliding scale that SDAT says delivered over $58 million in credits, with a $60,000 household income ceiling.
  • Property tax deferral: open to owners 65 or older where the local government has adopted it. The deferred amount becomes a lien and is repaid on transfer.

Religious, charitable and educational organizations may be exempt on property they own and use, and so may government property.

What happens if Maryland property tax goes unpaid?

The county can sell the tax lien at public auction, but the homeowner stays the owner. The buyer receives a tax lien certificate and may later ask a court to foreclose the right of redemption.

At least 30 days before the first advertisement, the Collector mails the owner of record a notice of the taxes owed. The sale is then advertised weekly for four successive weeks. A buyer can file a foreclosure case no earlier than six months after the sale, or nine months for owner-occupied homes under state law and in Baltimore City, and must file within two years of the certificate date or it becomes void.

The owner can redeem until the court forecloses, by paying the sale price, interest, later taxes and penalties in certified funds. If redemption happens more than four months after the sale, the owner also reimburses the certificate holder's expenses and attorney's fees. SDAT's State Tax Sale Ombudsman can be reached at (833) 732-8411.

How do back taxes affect selling a Maryland house?

Unpaid property tax is a lien, and a tax sale starts from that lien. Some counties also include water, sewer or special charges in it.

Owners who are behind should ask the county for the exact payoff and sale date, and owners already past a sale should ask the Ombudsman or the county about the redemption figure and the date, because costs rise the longer the lien sits.

When are Maryland property taxes due?

They are due July 1 and can be paid without interest through September 30. Owner-occupied homes can use a semiannual plan, with the second installment due December 1.

How long do I have to appeal my Maryland assessment?

You have 45 days from the date on the assessment notice. The next appeal goes to the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board within 30 days of the final notice.

How often does Maryland reassess property?

Every three years. Increases are phased in evenly over three years, and decreases take effect immediately.

Do I lose my house if I miss a property tax payment?

Not right away. The county sells the tax lien, and the owner keeps the property and can redeem it until a court forecloses the right of redemption.

Can a buyer appeal an assessment after purchase?

Yes, for a transfer between January 1 and June 30. The buyer files a Petition for Review within 60 days of the transfer, after the deed is recorded.

Who sets the tax rate in Maryland?

Each state, county and municipal government sets its own rate. The state does not limit property tax rates, but a proposed increase requires advertising and a public hearing.

What the official sources say

  • The Homestead Tax Credit limits the assessment increase on which tax is paid on the owner's principal residence; it is calculated on increases above the 10% State limit (or a lower local cap). (SDAT: Maryland Homestead Property Tax Credit Program; source)
  • The credit applies only when the annual assessment increase exceeds 10%. (SDAT: Maryland Homestead Property Tax Credit Program; source)
  • Homeowners must submit a one-time application to establish eligibility for the credit. (SDAT: Maryland Homestead Property Tax Credit Program; source)
  • The dwelling must be the owner's principal residence, lived in at least six months of the year including July 1; one property only; credit requires the property was not transferred to new ownership. (SDAT: Maryland Homestead Property Tax Credit Program; source)
  • Homeowners' Tax Credit (income-based): combined gross household income cannot exceed $60,000 and net worth (excluding the home and retirement accounts) must be under $200,000. (SDAT: Homeowners' Property Tax Credit Program; source)
  • Homeowners' Tax Credit application deadline is October 1 each year; apply by April 15 to have the credit on the tax bill; apply at least 30 days before settlement to receive credit at settlement. (SDAT: Homeowners' Property Tax Credit Program; source)
Selling in Maryland?
We buy Maryland houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What does the Maryland homestead exemption actually do?

In Maryland, the phrase usually points to the Homestead Property Tax Credit, which caps how fast the taxable assessment on your principal residence can rise. It does not take a fixed dollar amount off the value of your home.

The State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT) explains that every county and municipality must hold annual increases in taxable assessment to 10% or less. The credit only shows up on a bill in years when the phased-in assessment grows faster than the cap. In a flat year the owner may see no credit at all, and that does not mean the application was lost.

For a seller, the credit matters in two ways. It has been lowering the tax bill you carry now, and it does not travel with the house. A buyer has to qualify on their own after the deed is recorded.

How is the homestead credit calculated?

The credit equals the part of the assessment increase above the cap, multiplied by the tax rate. Under Tax-Property § 9-105(e), State and bicounty taxes use a fixed 110% of the prior year's taxable assessment, while each county or municipality picks a percentage between 100% and 110% for its own tax.

SDAT gives a worked example. An old assessment of $100,000 rises to a phased-in $120,000. A 10% cap allows $110,000, so $10,000 sits above the limit. At a rate of $1.04 per $100 of assessed value, the credit comes to $104.

StepExample figure
Prior taxable assessment$100,000
New phased-in assessment$120,000
Maximum allowed at a 10% cap$110,000
Amount above the cap$10,000
Rate used in the example$1.04 per $100
Credit on the bill$104

The statute also says credits under $1 are not granted. SDAT's page does not list each county's local cap, so check the county's current tax rate sheet for the percentage that applies to your address.

Who qualifies for the Maryland homestead credit?

You qualify if the house is your principal residence, you hold a legal interest in it, and nothing in the prior year disqualified the property. SDAT sets out these conditions:

  • You live in the home at least six months of the year, including July 1 of the credit year. Illness or a need for special care can excuse an absence.
  • You claim the credit on one property only.
  • The property was not transferred to new ownership in the prior tax year.
  • The owner did not request a zoning change that raised the value, and the use of the property did not change substantially.
  • The prior assessment was not clearly erroneous.

Section 9-105 defines a homeowner broadly. Sole ownership, joint ownership, tenancy by the entireties, a cooperative membership, a land installment contract and a life estate can all count as a legal interest.

There are carve-outs. If an accident or natural disaster damages the home, eligibility can continue for the current year and two more. An owner who razes the house or makes substantial improvements keeps eligibility by having lived there as a principal residence for at least three full tax years before the work, and by finishing within the next tax year. Federal employees stationed outside Maryland can also keep it for up to six consecutive years.

How do you apply, and how can you check your status?

You file one application, and it carries forward as long as you keep qualifying. A 2007 law (Tax-Property § 9-105) created the one-time requirement, and SDAT says the Maryland One Stop portal has taken applications since September 11, 2023.

  • Apply online at Maryland One Stop or through SDAT's homestead site.
  • Download the paper form in English or Spanish and mail it to the Homestead Tax Credit Division, 700 East Pratt Street, 2nd Floor, Suite 2700, Baltimore, MD 21202, or fax it to 410-225-9344.
  • Do not email an application that contains a Social Security number or a tax return.
  • Look up your property in SDAT's Real Property search. A status of Approved or Application Received needs no action, while No Application means you should file.

SDAT's questions line is 410-767-2165 in the Baltimore area and 1-866-650-8783 elsewhere in Maryland. A final denial can be appealed within 30 days to the Property Tax Assessment Appeal Board for the property's jurisdiction. SDAT's page lists no filing deadline for the application, although the text of § 9-105 as reproduced by Justia refers to May 1, so do not wait.

What happens to the homestead credit when you sell a Maryland house?

The credit ends for you at the sale, because a transfer for consideration disqualifies the property for the following year. The new owner must file their own application.

Maryland tries to make that hand-off hard to miss. Since 2021 (Chapter 333), a residential sales contract must carry a statement that a buyer who plans to live in the home may qualify for the homestead property tax credit, plus the SDAT web address. Under § 9-105(f), the settlement agent must present the buyer with the application document at settlement, and SDAT mails an application to new owners once the deed is recorded and its records update.

One timing rule helps in a few sales. If a deed is dated in one year but recorded between July 1 and September 1 of the next, the buyer can ask SDAT to treat the deed date as the transfer date. The request is due by September 1 of the second year after the deed date and must include a copy of the executed deed.

If you inherit the house, different rules apply, covered next.

What about heirs and the income-based Homeowners' Tax Credit?

Heirs who are not yet on the record title may qualify for the Homeowners' Tax Credit for up to three taxable years while the title transfer is finalized, according to SDAT. They need the will, trust or other instrument, a death certificate, proof of relationship, and the names and addresses of all heirs. The page also refers to an affidavit for continued credits for heirs tied to House Bill 1148 (2026).

The Homeowners' Tax Credit is a separate program with its own tests. Combined gross household income cannot exceed $60,000, and net worth, not counting the home or qualified retirement savings, must be under $200,000. Only tax on the first $300,000 of assessed value counts, and water and sewer charges are not covered.

Household incomeTax limit
$8,000$0
$12,000$160
$16,000$420
$20,000$780
$25,000$1,230
$30,000$1,680

The credit is the amount by which your property tax exceeds that limit. SDAT's chart is labeled 2025, so confirm current figures. Apply by April 15 to see the credit on the July bill. The filing deadline is October 1 each year. Buyers should apply at least 30 days before settlement to receive the credit at the closing table.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maryland houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Is there a homestead exemption against creditors in Maryland?

The exemptions in Courts and Judicial Proceedings § 11-504 are small, and the one for an owner-occupied home applies only in bankruptcy. A debtor can elect up to $6,000 in cash or property within 30 days of attachment or levy, and up to $500 in a bank account is exempt without electing, with the two combined capped at $6,000.

In a bankruptcy case, § 11-504 also covers owner-occupied residential property, including a condominium or cooperative unit used as a home, up to the federal amount in 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(1) adjusted for inflation. Spouses cannot both claim it in the same case, and an eight-year lookback applies to earlier successful claims on the same property.

This is a different idea from the tax credit, and the two are easy to confuse. A seller facing judgments, liens or a pending bankruptcy should talk with a Maryland attorney before signing a contract.

What are the penalties for claiming the credit wrongly?

A person who does not qualify must pay all the property tax otherwise due for each year of ineligibility. Willful misrepresentation adds a penalty of 25% of the credit received for each affected year, and that penalty becomes a lien on the property.

That lien is why a seller should confirm the status of a former second home or a rented-out house before listing. SDAT asks owners to report a property that has stopped being a principal residence to the local assessment office by email or phone. A lien of that kind is a title issue that has to be cleared before the sale can close.

How does the credit fit into selling a Maryland house for cash?

A cash sale does not change the tax rules, but it does shorten the window to clean them up. Before you accept an offer, gather three items: your latest tax bill, the SDAT property record showing your homestead status, and any notice about a prior-year credit.

  • Ask SDAT or your local assessment office whether the status shows Approved.
  • Check whether any tax is unpaid or any credit has been reversed.
  • If you are an heir, confirm whether you are on the record title yet.

Because the credit does not transfer, your buyer's first bill after closing can look different from yours. That is normal and reflects the buyer's own application, not an error in the sale.

More questions about Maryland Homestead Exemption

Does Maryland have a homestead exemption?

Maryland has a Homestead Property Tax Credit rather than a flat exemption. It limits yearly increases in the taxable assessment on your principal residence to 10% or less, and local governments may set a lower cap.

Do I have to reapply for the Maryland homestead credit every year?

No. SDAT says the homestead application is a one-time filing. The separate Homeowners' Tax Credit is different and is applied for each year, with an October 1 deadline.

Does the homestead credit transfer to the buyer when I sell?

No. A sale for consideration disqualifies the property for the following year, so the buyer must file a new application. The settlement agent is required to give the buyer the application at closing.

How do I know if I already have the credit?

Search the property in SDAT's Real Property database. Approved or Application Received means no action is needed, and No Application means you should file.

What if my homestead application is denied?

Contact SDAT's central homestead office to ask about the denial. A final denial can be appealed within 30 days to the Property Tax Assessment Appeal Board in the property's jurisdiction.

Can I keep the credit on a house I inherited?

Possibly for a limited time. Heirs not yet on the record title may qualify for the Homeowners' Tax Credit for up to three taxable years while title is finalized, with documents such as the will and death certificate.

content:
Maryland Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

What the official sources say

  • The Maryland estate tax exclusion for decedents dying on or after January 1, 2019 is $5.0 million. (Comptroller: Filing the Estate Tax Return; source)
  • An estate tax return is required if the federal gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts equals or exceeds the exemption amount and the decedent was a Maryland resident or owned Maryland real or tangible property. (Comptroller: Filing the Estate Tax Return; source)
  • Estate tax payment is due nine months after date of death, regardless of any extension. (Comptroller: Estate and Inheritance Tax Information; source)
  • Maryland inheritance tax is 10% on property passing to other individuals. (Comptroller: Estate and Inheritance Tax Information; source)
  • Property passing to a child or lineal descendant, spouse, parent, grandparent, stepchild, stepparent, or sibling is exempt from inheritance tax. (Comptroller: Estate and Inheritance Tax Information; source)
Selling in Maryland?
We buy Maryland houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How do the Maryland estate tax and the inheritance tax differ?

Maryland runs two separate death taxes. The estate tax is charged on the estate as a whole, while the inheritance tax is charged on what each person receives. A house can trigger one, both or neither, depending on the size of the estate and on who ends up owning it.

The legislature's 2026 fiscal note for Senate Bill 211 describes the estate tax as applying to the estates of Maryland residents and to nonresidents who own Maryland real property or tangible personal property located in the state. It says the rates come from a federal credit schedule as it stood on December 31, 2001, with a top marginal rate of 16 percent above $10,040,000 of adjusted taxable estate. Inheritance tax paid in Maryland can be credited against the estate tax.

The inheritance tax works from the other direction. Under Tax-General § 7-202, it is a tax on the privilege of receiving property from a deceased person when that property has a taxable situs in Maryland, so the recipient is the one the tax reaches.

What is the Maryland estate tax exclusion for each year of death?

For a death in 2019 or later, the exclusion is $5,000,000 plus any unused exclusion carried over from a deceased spouse. Tax-General § 7-309 sets the schedule, which stepped up gradually before that.

Year of deathExclusion amount
Before 2015$1,000,000
2015$1,500,000
2016$2,000,000
2017$3,000,000
2018$4,000,000
2019 and later$5,000,000 plus deceased spousal unused exclusion

The same section bars a deduction for state death taxes under federal code section 2058, and it caps the federal credit used in the Maryland calculation at 16 percent of the taxable estate above the exclusion. If a federal return is required, or would be required under the lower Maryland exclusion, § 7-305 puts the Maryland return due nine months after death. A return filed only to elect the spouse's unused exclusion follows the federal deadline for that election. An amended return is due within 90 days after the filer learns of an increase in tax.

Does Maryland give a break to estates that include a family farm?

Yes, up to $5,000,000 of qualified agricultural property can be left out of the gross estate if it passes to a qualified recipient who agrees to keep farming it. This matters on the Eastern Shore and in Western Maryland, where a farmhouse and its land are often one parcel.

If the farm property is worth more than $5,000,000, § 7-309(c) adds a second layer: 16 percent on the taxable estate above the exclusion (leaving the farm out of that figure), plus 5 percent of the farm value above $5,000,000. If the land stops being farmed within 10 years of the death, extra tax is recaptured. The inheritance tax has its own farmland rule: real property under a perpetual farming easement that passes to a niece or nephew is exempt, with recapture if farming ends.

Heirs who inherit a farmhouse and want to sell it to someone who will not farm should ask the estate's attorney whether either recapture rule is in play before any contract is signed.

Who pays the 10 percent Maryland inheritance tax?

People who are not close family pay it. Tax-General § 7-204 sets the rate at 10 percent of the clear value of property passing from the decedent, and clear value is fair market value minus expenses.

Section 7-203(b) exempts property passing to a long list of relatives. The Register of Wills page for inheritance tax fills in who is taxed and who is not:

RecipientTreatment
Spouse, parent, grandparent, child, stepchild, sibling, lineal descendantsExempt (§ 7-203(b))
Niece, nephew, aunt, uncle, cousinTaxed at 10 percent (nieces and nephews are exempt only for easement farmland)
Friend or unrelated individualTaxed at 10 percent, subject to listed exceptions
Registered domestic partner (death on or after October 1, 2023)Exempt
Other domestic partner (death on or after July 1, 2009)Taxed, except a primary residence held jointly with survivorship, with an affidavit or two proofs of partnership
Qualifying 501(c)(3) charity; State, county or municipalityExempt

A corporation, partnership or LLC owned entirely by exempt relatives is also exempt. For a will beneficiary, most wills carry a tax clause that makes the estate pay. Without one, the legatee pays, and an heir in an intestate estate pays personally.

What property is exempt from the Maryland inheritance tax?

Several categories of property are outside the tax no matter who receives them. Section 7-203 and the Register of Wills list these:

  • Life insurance paid to a named beneficiary other than the estate
  • Up to $500 left in a will for grave upkeep
  • Property passing to any one person if it totals $1,000 or less
  • Property distributed through a small estate under Estates and Trusts § 5-601
  • Income and gains on probate assets earned after the date of death
  • Qualifying public and private employee benefit plan payments
  • Personal property of nonresident decedents when reciprocity applies, though not tangible property located in Maryland

The small estate exemption is the one that touches most homes with little equity. The Register of Wills pamphlet defines a small estate as probate assets of $50,000 or less, or $100,000 or less when the spouse is the sole heir or legatee, valued at fair market value less debts secured by the property.

How does the Register of Wills collect the inheritance tax?

The Register of Wills in the relevant county determines and collects it. When an estate is administered in court, the personal representative files an Administration Account that shows who received what, and the payment goes in with that account.

When property passes outside probate, the Register sends an invoice based on the Information Report or an Application to Fix Inheritance Tax. Under § 7-214, if there is no formal administration, the Register in the county where the inventory is filed makes the determination and sends a bill to each person responsible. The Register's collection schedule for those invoices runs like this:

  • After 30 days without payment, a 10 percent penalty and interest are added and a second invoice goes out.
  • At 60 days from the first invoice, more interest applies and a third invoice is sent.
  • At 90 days, the full amount goes to the Maryland Central Collection Unit, which may add interest at up to 18 percent.

Heirs who plan to sell the house should ask the Register what has been billed before they count on the proceeds.

What happens when an heir wants to sell an inherited Maryland house?

Nobody can sell estate property until the Register of Wills or the Orphans' Court has appointed a personal representative. The Register's administration pamphlet says this appointment must come before any asset is disposed of, and that if real property is sold, a copy of the closing disclosure goes in with the First Account.

The usual sequence, based on that pamphlet, looks like this:

  • File the original will with the Register of Wills in the county where the decedent lived.
  • Get a personal representative appointed.
  • File a List of Interested Persons within 20 days of appointment in a regular estate.
  • File the inventory within three months, listing the house at fair market value as of the date of death.
  • File the account, which is where inheritance tax is determined and paid.

Commissions for the personal representative are capped at 9 percent when the property is $20,000 or less, and at $1,800 plus 3.6 percent of the excess above that. Probate fees are charged when the First Account is filed, and they rise with the estate's size.

Is Maryland about to change its estate tax?

A repeal was proposed in 2026, but we could not confirm that it became law. Senate Bill 211 (2026 session, first reader) would have repealed the estate tax for decedents dying on or after July 1, 2026, and its fiscal note estimated a general fund revenue decrease of about $44.0 million in fiscal 2027 and about $182.5 million in fiscal 2028. The note does not describe any change to the inheritance tax.

The 2026 statute page for § 7-309 on the General Assembly site still shows the $5,000,000 exclusion text. Check the Comptroller's current guidance for the date of death in your family's case before relying on any figure above.

More questions about Maryland Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Maryland have an inheritance tax?

Yes. Maryland charges a 10 percent inheritance tax on the clear value of property passing to people who are not close relatives. Spouses, children, parents, grandparents, siblings and lineal descendants are exempt under Tax-General § 7-203(b).

Do children pay Maryland inheritance tax on an inherited house?

No. Property passing to a child, stepchild or other lineal descendant is exempt. A niece, nephew, cousin or friend who inherits the same house is taxed at 10 percent of its clear value.

When is the Maryland estate tax return due?

Nine months after the date of death, when a federal return is required or would be required under the lower Maryland exclusion. A return filed only to claim a spouse's unused exclusion follows the federal deadline for that election.

Can heirs sell an inherited Maryland house before the estate closes?

Yes, once a personal representative has been appointed. The Register of Wills requires that appointment before any asset is disposed of, and a copy of the closing disclosure is filed with the First Account.

What if the inheritance tax invoice goes unpaid?

The Register adds a 10 percent penalty and interest after 30 days, sends more invoices, and at 90 days refers the debt to the Central Collection Unit, which may charge interest at up to 18 percent.

Is a small estate exempt from Maryland inheritance tax?

Yes. Property distributed from an estate that qualifies as small under Estates and Trusts § 5-601 is exempt. The Register of Wills pamphlet sets that at $50,000 or less, or $100,000 or less if the spouse is the only heir or legatee.

What the official sources say

  • Before filing a failure-to-pay-rent case, the landlord must give written notice of intent (form DC-CV-115) stating rent due and giving 10 days to pay. (Maryland Courts: Housing Cases; source)
  • Breach-of-lease and tenant-holding-over cases allow eviction to be sought immediately after judgment. (Maryland Courts: Housing Cases; source)
  • The landlord requests a Warrant of Restitution within 60 days of judgment (failure to pay rent) and must notify the tenant of the eviction date at least 6 days before. (Maryland Courts: Housing Cases; source)
  • A foreclosure sale may not occur until at least 45 days after service of process when the property is not owner-occupied. (Real Property Art. 7-105.1(n); source)

What are the steps of a Maryland eviction, in order?

A Maryland eviction runs through the District Court in the county where the property sits, and it cannot end with a sheriff at the door unless the landlord first wins a judgment and obtains a warrant. Both the Maryland Courts help page and the state tenant guidance describe the same basic sequence for a rent case:

  1. The landlord sends the written notice of intent and waits out the 10-day cure period.
  2. The landlord files a sworn complaint and the court issues a summons.
  3. A rent court hearing takes place, usually on a short schedule.
  4. If the landlord wins, the tenant has a short window to leave or pay.
  5. The landlord petitions for a warrant of restitution, with no hearing.
  6. The landlord gives the final written notice of the eviction date.
  7. A sheriff or constable carries out the eviction.

The notice rules themselves are covered in our Maryland eviction notice guide. This page follows what happens once the case is in court.

Which kinds of landlord cases does the District Court hear?

Five. The Maryland Courts housing page lists them, along with the forms landlords use.

Case typeWhat it seeksForm or step
Failure to pay rentEviction and possibly back rentDC-CV-115 notice, then DC-CV-082 complaint
Tenant holding overEviction after the lease endsCourt complaint
Breach of leaseEviction for lease violationsCourt complaint
Wrongful detainerRemoval of someone who is not a lawful occupantCourt complaint
Petition for warrant of restitutionCarrying out a judgment already wonDC-CV-081, no hearing

Tenants have their own filings too, including rent escrow and breach of the warranty of habitability (DC-CV-083) and security deposit claims. Foreclosure cases belong to the circuit courts, not the District Court.

What happens at rent court?

For unpaid rent, the trial is set for the fifth day after the complaint is filed. Under Real Property § 8-401, the court may adjourn for one day to bring in witnesses, or longer if all parties agree.

The landlord generally speaks first and the tenant responds. The judge can rule on the spot or set another hearing. If someone does not show up, the court may dismiss, enter judgment or postpone. A tenant can ask for a postponement by writing to the clerk before trial and mailing a copy to the landlord.

Service matters here. An eviction-only case can proceed on mail plus posting on the property, but a money judgment for back rent requires personal service on a residential tenant. Posting can support a default judgment for possession and cannot support one for money owed.

If rent is truly due, the court fixes the amount owed as of the filing date and orders possession surrendered within 4 days after trial. A physician's certificate can stretch that to no more than 15 days. If the tenant pays the rent, late fees and costs at trial or at an adjourned date, the complaint is marked satisfied and there is no eviction.

Can a tenant stop an eviction after losing in court?

In most rent cases, yes, by paying what the judgment says before the eviction is carried out. This is called the right of redemption, and § 8-401(h) covers it. The tenant pays all past-due rent plus the costs and fees the court awarded.

  • Checks from a government agency or government-funded organization must be accepted by the landlord.
  • The Maryland Courts page lists cash, certified check and money order as accepted forms of payment.
  • A landlord can ask the court to deny redemption when the tenant has had three possession judgments for unpaid rent in the previous 12 months (four in Baltimore City, according to the court's guidance).

A tenant who wants the judgment reviewed can appeal to the circuit court within 4 days in a nonpayment case, and has to post a bond to stay in the home. In breach-of-lease and holdover cases the appeal window is 10 days.

When can the landlord ask for the warrant, and how long does it last?

The Maryland Courts help page tells landlords to wait 7 business days after a possession judgment in a failure-to-pay-rent case. Breach-of-lease and holdover judgments allow the request immediately. The statute states the waiting period as 7 days, so a landlord or tenant working from the text of § 8-401(f) should compare it with the court's current instructions.

There is also an expiry date. In a nonpayment case the landlord must order the warrant within 60 days of the later of the judgment or the end of any stay, or the possession judgment is stricken. The same happens if a warrant is ordered and nothing is done within 60 days. A stricken judgment can still count toward the number of judgments that eliminates redemption rights.

Once the warrant is in hand, the landlord must send the final notice at least 6 days ahead. If the sheriff has doubts about that notice, or the tenant may have redeemed, the sheriff must tell the District Court and wait for a further order.

What happens on eviction day in Maryland?

A sheriff or constable has to be present. The Maryland Courts page gives these ground rules:

  • No evictions on Sundays or holidays.
  • The landlord is not required to tell the tenant the exact day in advance, beyond the 6-day window notice.
  • Once belongings are removed, the tenant is responsible for them.
  • The sheriff checks for dogs or cats. If the tenant is present the animal is handed over, and if not, the sheriff provides shelter or rescue contact information.
  • Baltimore City has extra notice and property-removal rules.

Weather can postpone the day. For residential property, the warrant is stayed day to day during extreme weather, including temperatures of 32 degrees Fahrenheit or lower and certain National Weather Service winter, hurricane, tropical storm or excessive heat warnings. After conditions end, the eviction has to be finished within 5 days. Government employees furloughed during a shutdown may also qualify for a stay, generally no longer than 30 days past the shutdown's end.

If the tenant is not home, the officer posts a notice on the front door stating that repossession is complete. A tenant who proves the landlord broke the notice rules can recover actual damages, attorney's fees and injunctive relief.

What help exists for tenants, and why does it matter to an owner who wants to sell?

Tenants with household income at or below 50 percent of the state median may qualify for a free lawyer through the Access to Counsel in Evictions program, reached by calling 211. The Maryland Court Help Center takes calls at 410-260-1392, Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m.

An owner who is thinking of selling a rented house should know that the sale has its own tenant protections. Before listing a house with three or fewer units, an owner generally has to give a tenant of at least six months a written chance to offer, under § 8-119, with exceptions for foreclosure transfers, estate fiduciaries, inheritance and family sales.

A landlord also cannot force the issue. Section 8-216 bars lockouts and utility shutoffs, and the only lawful ways to regain possession are a court warrant carried out by a sheriff or constable or an abandonment or surrender by the tenant.

More questions about Maryland Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a Maryland eviction take?

The statutes set short steps rather than one total. A rent trial is set for the fifth day after filing, possession is due within 4 days after trial, the warrant request follows, and the landlord gives at least 6 days written notice before the sheriff acts. Postponements, appeals and weather stays add time.

Can a tenant pay and stay after a judgment?

Usually yes. A tenant can redeem by paying all past-due rent plus court-awarded costs and fees before the eviction is carried out. A landlord can ask the court to deny redemption after three possession judgments in 12 months (four in Baltimore City).

Which court handles evictions in Maryland?

The District Court in the county where the property is located. Circuit courts handle foreclosure cases and appeals from District Court landlord-tenant judgments.

Does the sheriff have to be there for an eviction?

Yes. A sheriff or constable carries out the warrant of restitution, and evictions are not allowed on Sundays or holidays.

Can a landlord sell a rented house while an eviction case is pending?

Yes, but tenant protections still apply. For a rental of three or fewer units, a tenant of six months or more generally gets a written chance to make an offer before the owner lists the property.

Is there free legal help for Maryland tenants facing eviction?

Yes. The Access to Counsel in Evictions program offers free lawyers to tenants at or below 50 percent of the state median income. Call 211, or reach the Maryland Court Help Center at 410-260-1392.

  • A TOD deed is effective if recorded in the land records of the property's county before the transferor's death. (HB 738 (2026), Estates & Trusts Art.; source)

Maryland Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Maryland rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Maryland?

It is a deed that names who gets a house when the owner dies, signed and recorded while the owner is alive. Maryland's version took effect October 1, 2026, under House Bill 738, Chapter 751 of the 2026 laws.

The new subtitle sits in Real Property Article 14-1001 and following. The owner stays in control for life: the deed gives the named beneficiary no ownership until death. The Daily Record's October 2026 explainer compares it to a beneficiary designation on a bank account or life insurance policy.

The Act applies to a deed made before, on or after October 1, 2026, if the owner dies on or after that date. The Daily Record advises talking with an estate planning attorney about drafting and recording, and about how the deed fits with a will and the rest of the plan.

  • Owner: called the transferor in the statute.
  • Beneficiary: the person or people named to receive the property.
  • Joint owners: owners with survivorship rights, such as tenants by the entirety, are treated differently from tenants in common.

Who can sign one and what must it say?

Any owner with the capacity needed to make a will can sign one. The deed must follow the execution rules in Estates and Trusts 4-101 and must state that the transfer to the beneficiary happens at the owner's death.

The statutory form in 14-1011 includes owner and beneficiary information, a legal description, the transfer-at-death statement, and preparer and notary sections. Its notes say witnesses and notaries cannot be relatives of the owners or beneficiaries, or beneficiaries themselves.

A deed can name one beneficiary or several. If it names several and does not say how they hold title, they take as joint tenants with rights of survivorship. A deed can also name alternate beneficiaries, including successive alternates, who take if a primary beneficiary does not survive the owner.

How is a Maryland TOD deed recorded and taxed?

It must be recorded in the land records of the county where the house sits before the owner dies, or it has no effect. Signing it is not enough.

Recording follows Real Property 3-104 with several changes the Act makes for TOD deeds. The collector's endorsement, certain intake sheet and assessment office endorsements, and the attorney or party preparation certification do not apply. The clerk may still refuse a TOD deed that comes without an intake sheet. The assessment records do not change to the beneficiary's name until the owner's death.

ItemRule under Chapter 751
When it takes effectAt the owner's death, if recorded before then
Notice to beneficiaryNot required during the owner's life
ConsiderationNot required
State recordation tax and state and county transfer taxExempt if primary or secondary residence of the owner
Inheritance taxBeneficiaries may still owe it, per the form's informational sheet

The enrolled bill cites Tax-Property 12-108, 13-207 and 13-414 for these exemptions.

What can the owner still do while alive?

Almost everything. The deed does not change the owner's right to live in, sell or mortgage the house, and it does not give the beneficiary a legal or equitable interest.

Section 14-1007 lists what a recorded TOD deed does not do during the owner's life.

  • It does not limit the owner's right to sell or encumber the property.
  • It does not affect a buyer's or lender's rights, even if they know about the deed.
  • It does not affect the rights of the owner's creditors, including future ones.
  • It does not affect eligibility for public assistance, including Medicaid, for the owner or the beneficiary.
  • It does not expose the house to claims by the beneficiary's creditors.

The Daily Record notes this is a difference from adding a relative to the title as a joint owner, which can expose the house to that person's creditors, lawsuits or divorce and gives them present rights.

How is a TOD deed changed or revoked?

By recording a new document before the owner dies. A TOD deed is always revocable, even if the deed itself says otherwise.

There are three ways to revoke all or part of a recorded deed, each recorded in the county land records.

  • A new TOD deed that expressly revokes the earlier one or conflicts with it.
  • An instrument of revocation that says so expressly.
  • A lifetime deed that expressly revokes the TOD deed.

A will cannot revoke a recorded TOD deed, and neither can marking up the deed itself. With joint owners, a deed is revoked only if all living joint owners revoke. The statutory form notes that a TOD deed naming a spouse is revoked automatically by divorce or annulment, and that it is also revoked if the owner later marries and has a child by birth, adoption or legitimation.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maryland houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens when the owner dies?

Title passes to the surviving beneficiary by operation of law, without probate for that house. The beneficiary takes subject to any existing mortgage, lien, security interest or encumbrance, and the transfer carries no warranty of title.

If a beneficiary does not survive the owner, that share lapses, and an alternate takes if one is named. A beneficiary who intentionally killed the owner is disqualified, and the Act keeps the rights of pretermitted children and the elective share of a spouse in play. Any beneficiary may disclaim, and for real property the disclaimer must be recorded in the county land records.

Section 14-1013 creates an optional Notification of Death form. The statute sets no deadline to record it, and the transfer happens at death whether or not it is recorded. Recording it still matters, because the clerk forwards it to the State Department of Assessments and Taxation so the property records can be updated. If a beneficiary who lives in the house uses the form's occupancy option, the beneficiary certifies under penalty of perjury to live there as a principal residence for at least 7 of the next 12 months.

How does a TOD deed affect selling the house?

The owner can sell the house any time while alive without the beneficiary's consent. After death, the beneficiary can sell once title has passed and the paperwork is in order.

A beneficiary who inherits through a TOD deed takes a house with whatever debt is attached. A buyer or title company may ask to see the recorded TOD deed and the notification of death, if one was recorded.

Cash Home Buyers buys Maryland houses as-is, including inherited homes. If you are a beneficiary and the house needs repairs or has back taxes, call us before you spend money on repairs. If you are an owner thinking about a TOD deed and a sale, remember that the deed does not stop you from selling while you are alive.

The Daily Record lists tax effects, existing liens, multiple beneficiaries, possible family disputes and Medicaid or long-term care planning among the points to check before relying on a TOD deed.

More questions about Maryland Transfer on Death Deed

When did Maryland's transfer on death deed take effect?

October 1, 2026, under House Bill 738 (Chapter 751 of the 2026 laws). It covers deeds made before, on or after that date if the owner dies on or after it.

Does a TOD deed have to be recorded?

Yes. It is effective only if recorded in the land records of the county where the property is located before the owner's death.

Can I still sell my house if I record a TOD deed?

Yes. The deed does not limit your right to sell or mortgage the property, and it does not give the beneficiary any interest while you are alive.

Does a will override a TOD deed in Maryland?

No. A recorded TOD deed cannot be revoked by a will. It can be revoked by a recorded new TOD deed, a recorded revocation, or a recorded lifetime deed.

Does a TOD deed avoid inheritance tax?

No. The recordation and transfer taxes are exempt for a residence, but beneficiaries may still owe inheritance tax, according to the informational sheet with the form.

What taxes make up Maryland seller closing costs?

Three government charges drive most Maryland closing statements: the State transfer tax, a county transfer tax and a recordation tax. The State transfer tax is 0.5% of the consideration, and the county taxes vary by county.

These are charges on the deed, so they appear whether or not a real estate agent is involved. A recording fee and a surcharge are added by the Clerk of the Circuit Court, and the property tax account has to be clear before the deed is accepted.

  • State transfer tax: 0.5% of consideration, collected by the Circuit Court clerk.
  • County transfer tax: set by each county, from 0% to 1.5% in the Department of Legislative Services table.
  • Recordation tax: set by each county per $500 of consideration.
  • Recording fee and surcharge: charged by the clerk for each instrument.
  • Property tax and other county charges due: paid before the transfer is entered.

Who pays the transfer and recordation taxes in Maryland?

Under Real Property Article 14-104, recordation tax and the State and local transfer taxes are presumed to be shared equally between buyer and seller unless the contract or the law says otherwise. Most Maryland contracts address this directly, so read the clause before you sign.

There is one major exception. When the buyer is a first-time Maryland buyer who will occupy the house as a principal residence, the seller pays all of the State transfer tax, and also the recordation and local transfer tax unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

Several conditions apply to that rule. Each buyer on the deed must sign a statement under oath, and with two or more buyers every one of them must qualify. The first-time buyer State transfer tax rate is 0.25% rather than 0.5%, which cuts the seller's share of that line.

Recordation tax law also lets a local government exempt an amount for owner-occupied homes when the buyer lives there at least 7 months of a 12 month period. Ask the clerk or your title company whether your county does.

How much do transfer and recordation taxes differ between Maryland counties?

County rates differ a lot, so the same price can produce very different bills. The Department of Legislative Services lists fiscal 2026 rates for each jurisdiction.

Montgomery County varies by property value and adds a recordation surcharge on transactions over $500,000. Anne Arundel's transfer tax runs from 1.0% to 1.5%. Statewide, recordation runs from $2.50 to $7.00 per $500, and the transfer tax from 0% to 1.5%.

What would the taxes be on a $400,000 Maryland house?

If the buyer and seller split these equally under the default rule, each side carries half. If the buyer qualifies as a first-time Maryland buyer, the State transfer tax falls to 0.25% and the seller covers the full set unless the contract says otherwise.

What recording fees and surcharges does the clerk add?

The Clerk of the Circuit Court charges a recording fee of $20 for most deeds of nine pages or less and a $40 surcharge on nearly every recorded instrument. Both Harford and Howard County list the same figures.

  • Release of nine pages or less: $10.
  • Instrument of ten pages or more that is not a principal residence: $75.
  • Copies: $0.50 a page in Harford County, plus $5 for a certified copy.
  • Harford Land Records e-records through Simplifile.

Recording fees are non-refundable, and State transfer tax refunds need a claim form returned to the clerk. When a tax exemption applies, the document must cite the full exemption code. Without it, the clerk charges full tax.

What property tax steps come before a Maryland deed transfers?

Real Property Article 3-104 requires property taxes, assessments and charges due to be paid, with the collector's certificate endorsed on the deed, before the transfer is entered on the assessment books. A county or municipality may charge up to $55 for a certificate of paid charges in certain counties.

Counties set their own procedure. Harford County sells a Certificate of Tax Liens and Other Charges Due for $50 that is valid 90 days, and county staff stamp every deed before recording. In Howard County, deeds go through the Department of Finance's Division of Recordation Tax before they reach Land Records.

Unpaid tax is the line most likely to surprise a seller. Maryland sells liens at annual tax sales, and an owner can redeem a property by paying the lien, interest and fees any time before a circuit judge signs a foreclosure order.

Where do the county steps happen and how long do they take?

Each county has two stops: a county tax office that collects and stamps, and the Circuit Court land records office that records the deed. Two sample counties show how the hours and timing differ.

  • Harford: Revenue Collections at 220 S. Main Street, Bel Air, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, with processing that usually takes 24 to 48 hours.
  • Harford Land Records: 20 West Courtland Street, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with a 4:00 p.m. courier and title company cutoff.
  • Howard: Division of Recordation Tax at 3430 Courthouse Drive, Ellicott City, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • Howard Land Records: 9250 Judicial Way, Suite 1900, with recording hours of 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.

Harford walk-ins are limited to five documents or sets at a time.

What about sellers who live out of state?

A nonresident individual seller has 8.75% of the total sale payment withheld at settlement, and a nonresident entity has 8.25% withheld. Form MW506NRS reports it, and the deed cannot be recorded without the payment.

The withholding is an advance on income tax, not a closing cost in the normal sense. If you owe less, you can apply for an early refund when the price is below $1.5 million. See our Maryland capital gains guide for the full rules.

How do closing costs work in a direct cash sale?

The same taxes and fees apply to a cash sale as to a financed one, because they are charges on the deed and on the tax account. What changes is who agrees to pay which item in the contract.

Before you sign anything, ask for a written net sheet that lists each tax line. Check three things: whether the buyer claims first-time buyer status, who pays the county transfer tax and recordation tax, and what the county shows as owed on the tax account. Your title company or attorney can confirm each one.

More questions about Maryland Closing Costs for Sellers

Who pays the Maryland transfer tax?

Unless the contract says otherwise, buyer and seller split the State and local transfer taxes and the recordation tax equally. When a first-time Maryland buyer will live in the house, the seller pays all of the State transfer tax and, by default, the local taxes too.

What is the Maryland State transfer tax rate?

It is 0.5% of the consideration. For a first-time Maryland buyer who will occupy the house as a principal residence, the rate is 0.25% and the seller pays all of it.

How much is the recordation tax in Maryland?

Each county sets it per $500 of consideration. The legislature's table lists $2.50 in Howard and Baltimore Counties, $3.30 in Harford, and $7.00 in Frederick.

Do Maryland sellers pay a recording fee?

The clerk charges $20 for most deeds of nine pages or less and a $40 surcharge. Whether the buyer or seller covers it depends on the contract.

Is property tax paid before closing in Maryland?

Yes. Taxes, assessments and charges due must be paid, with the collector's certificate endorsed on the deed, before the transfer is entered on the assessment books.

What the official sources say

  • Real property may be valued for the inventory at its tax-assessment full cash value or at the arm's-length contract sales price if settlement occurs within one year of death. (Register of Wills: Administration of Estates; source)
  • Creditor claims must be presented within the earlier of six months after death or 30 days after notice to the creditor. (Register of Wills: Administration of Estates; source)
  • Residential property from a decedent's estate to an heir may be recorded with a payment plan for taxes due instead of full payment of taxes. (Real Property Art. 3-104; source)
Selling in Maryland?
We buy Maryland houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Who handles probate in Maryland?

Each of Maryland's 24 jurisdictions has its own Register of Wills and its own Orphans' Court. The 24 are the state's 23 counties and Baltimore City, and you file in the jurisdiction where the person who died lived.

The Register is an elected official, chosen every four years, who handles the paperwork of administrative probate. The Orphans' Court steps in for disputes and for judicial probate. In Harford, Howard and Montgomery Counties a Circuit Court judge serves as the Orphans' Court, and the other 21 jurisdictions elect three judges to four-year terms.

For a family selling an inherited house, the first step is finding the right office, and the Registers of Wills website lists them by county.

What kinds of estates does Maryland recognize?

Maryland sorts estates into small, regular, modified and judicial, and the label depends on asset value, who inherits and whether anyone contests the will. The Registers of Wills describe the dividing lines this way.

TypeWho it fitsNotable features
Small estateProbate assets of $50,000 or less, or $100,000 or less if the spouse is the only heir or legateeNo fee to file the petition, and no inheritance tax collected on probate property
Regular estateProbate assets above those amountsInventory, accounts and a fuller notice process
Modified administrationA solvent regular estate for a death on or after October 1, 1997, where residual takers are the personal representative and certain tax-exempt people or entitiesFinal report instead of an inventory and accounts
Judicial probateCases where the will is questioned or damaged, or more than one qualified person appliesRun by the Orphans' Court

The Registers count assets in the decedent's sole name or held as tenants in common as probate assets. Anything that passes another way is a question for the Register or an attorney.

What are the steps and deadlines in a regular estate?

A regular estate follows a fixed calendar that starts with the petition and runs about nine months to the first account. Here are the milestones the Register of Wills lists:

  • File the original will with the Register, then the Petition for Administration (Form 1112) and Schedule A (Form 1136), promptly after death.
  • File the List of Interested Persons with the petition or within 20 days of appointment.
  • Publish the Notice of Appointment for three consecutive weeks and supply copies for mailing within 20 days.
  • File the inventory and information report within three months of appointment.
  • File the first account within nine months.

Small estates move faster. The information report is due within three months of appointment, and where no formal administration is opened an Application to Fix Tax on Non-Probate Assets is due within 90 days of death. Modified administration compresses the ending, with a final report due within 10 months and distribution within 12.

Can a personal representative sell the house without court approval?

Usually yes. Under Estates and Trusts § 7-401, a personal representative can act without court approval and may sell, mortgage, exchange or lease estate property, unless the will limits those powers.

The catch is timing. Duties and powers begin when the Register issues Letters of Administration. A family member who has not been appointed cannot sign a deed on the estate's behalf,, so the Letters come before any deed.

The same section lets a personal representative keep assets until sale, pay valid claims, insure property, pay funeral, tax and administration costs, and borrow money. Registers of Wills describe the personal representative's role as fiduciary and held to the highest standard of care, with possible personal liability for falling short.

How is an inherited house valued for the inventory?

For a regular estate, real property can be valued at its full cash value for property tax assessment, or at the arm's-length contract sales price if settlement happens within one year of death. That second option is the one that matters when you sell quickly.

Small estates use fair market value less debts of record secured by the property at death. Appraisals containing words such as approximate are not accepted for the inventory, and values are as of the date of death. Assessment values cannot be used for farmland, woodland or land on a national registry.

Maryland also lets residential property from an estate pass to an heir with taxes due at recording paid under a payment plan, under Real Property § 3-104. If the heir sells soon after, the plan and the title steps should be cleared up with the settlement company.

Who can serve as personal representative, and is a bond required?

Most adults can serve, with a few exclusions, and a bond is often part of the process. Disqualified people include anyone under 18, a person found mentally incompetent, those with certain serious convictions unless good cause is shown, and non-citizens unless they are permanent residents who are a spouse, ancestor, descendant or sibling of the decedent.

  • A nonresident must file an irrevocable designation of a Maryland resident agent (Form 1106).
  • In a small estate, a bond (Form 1115) is required when the estate is $10,000 or more after allowable expenses, unless the will excuses it or all interested persons waive it.
  • In a regular estate, a nominal bond is used when bond is excused or waived, and an insurance company must execute any bond.

Anyone holding the original will must deposit it with the Register promptly after death. A custodian who willfully refuses to deliver a will after notice of death can be liable for resulting damages.

How are creditors paid before heirs?

Creditors get paid first, in a legal order, and the house may have to be sold to cover them. A claim must be presented by the earlier of six months after death or 30 days after the creditor receives written notice that the claim will be barred. The Department of Health has its own period, running to the earlier of six months after the appointment notice is published or two months after it receives notice.

If the estate cannot pay everyone, the Registers list this order:

  • Register fees, then administration costs and expenses
  • Funeral expenses up to $15,000
  • Personal representative compensation, legal services and real estate broker commissions
  • Family allowance, child support and the decedent's taxes
  • Last-illness bills, up to three months of rent arrears, and wages from the final three months

Debts owed to the federal government, such as IRS taxes, have absolute priority under federal law.

What does probate cost in Maryland?

Fees rise with the value of the estate, and the inheritance tax depends on who receives the property. The probate fee is $0 for an estate under $50,000, $100 from $50,000 to under $100,000, $200 from $100,000 to under $500,000, and $1,000 from $500,000 to under $1 million.

Personal representative and attorney compensation is capped at 9% of the first $20,000 plus 3.6% of the value above $20,000, though an attorney can petition for more for good cause. Funeral expenses up to $15,000 can be paid without a court order when the estate is solvent and the will allows it. A surviving spouse or registered domestic partner receives a $10,000 family allowance, and each unmarried minor child receives $5,000.

Maryland's inheritance tax has a 10% collateral rate for recipients outside the exempt groups, which include spouses, children, parents, grandparents, siblings and their lineal descendants. The first $1,000 passing to any one person is exempt.

What do heirs face when they want to sell the house fast?

Heirs usually face a gap between wanting to sell and having legal authority to do so. Until a personal representative is appointed, nobody holds the powers that Estates and Trusts § 7-401 describes.

Selling as-is to a cash buyer can take repairs off the family's list, but the personal representative still has to follow the notice and claims calendar above. Keep the Letters, the death certificate and any bond paperwork together for the closing.

More questions about Maryland Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

How long does probate take in Maryland?

A regular estate follows a schedule of about nine months to the first account, and a modified administration is designed to close in about 13 months. Contested or complicated estates run longer.

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house in Maryland?

Generally yes, if the house was in the decedent's sole name. The personal representative's authority begins when Letters of Administration are issued, and the Register issues them after the petition is processed.

Can the personal representative sell the house without asking the court?

Usually. Estates and Trusts § 7-401 lets a personal representative sell estate property without court approval unless the will limits that power.

What is a small estate in Maryland?

It is an estate with probate assets of $50,000 or less, or $100,000 or less when the surviving spouse is the sole heir or legatee. There is no filing fee, and no inheritance tax is collected on probate property.

How long do creditors have to file claims?

The deadline is the earlier of six months after death or 30 days after the creditor receives written notice that the claim will be barred.

Does Maryland charge an inheritance tax?

Yes, on certain recipients. Spouses, children, parents, grandparents and siblings are exempt, and the collateral rate is 10% for others, with the first $1,000 to any one person exempt.

What the official sources say

  • Maryland personal income tax rates start at 2% on the first $1,000 and rise to a maximum of 5.75% (tax year 2021 page). (Comptroller: Tax Information for Individual Income Tax; source)
  • Maryland's 23 counties and Baltimore City levy a local income tax collected on the resident state return. (Comptroller: Tax Information for Individual Income Tax; source)
  • Nonresidents are subject to a special tax rate of 2.25% in addition to the state income tax rate (tax year 2021 page). (Comptroller: Tax Information for Individual Income Tax; source)
  • Nonresident sellers of real property are subject to withholding of 8.75% (individuals) or 8.25% (entities) of the sale payment. (Comptroller: Employer Withholding; source)
Selling in Maryland?
We buy Maryland houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Maryland have its own capital gains tax on a house sale?

Maryland has no separate capital gains rate for most sellers: gain from a house is added to income and taxed at the regular state rates, plus a local income tax. Starting with tax year 2025, an extra 2% applies to net capital gains for people whose federal adjusted gross income is above $350,000.

Before that change, the Comptroller's Technical Bulletin 58 notes, capital gains were taxed at the same rate as ordinary income. The new 2% sits on top of the regular tax, so a seller above the threshold pays both. Corporations are not subject to it. A pass-through entity does not pay it, though an owner who receives a gain from one can, and a trust or estate with federal taxable income over $350,000 owes it on undistributed gains.

Most Maryland homeowners selling a primary residence never meet the surtax, because the bulletin excludes that gain when it applies. The details are in the next sections.

Which Maryland house sales are excluded from the extra 2% tax?

A primary residence that sells for less than $1.5 million is excluded from the 2% surtax. The excluded property types are a single-family home, townhome, row home, or residential condo or co-op unit, including the land and any accessory dwelling unit.

The same bulletin lists several other exclusions that are less relevant to a house seller but worth knowing:

  • Gain held in retirement accounts such as a 401(k) or IRA.
  • Land under a conservation, agricultural or forest preservation easement.
  • Gain deferred in a like-kind exchange under IRC section 1031, because it is not in federal AGI.
  • Affordable housing owned by a nonprofit.

A rental house, a second home or an inherited house that was never your residence does not fit the primary residence description in the bulletin, so for a seller above the $350,000 line the gain on it can be subject to the extra 2%.

What Maryland income tax rates apply to the gain?

Maryland's top brackets for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 are 5.75%, 6.25% and 6.5%, based on income. Lower brackets start at 2% on the first $1,000, per the Comptroller's individual income tax page, which also notes the county and Baltimore City local tax.

State rateSingle filersJoint filers and heads of household
5.75%$250,001 to $500,000$300,001 to $600,000
6.25%$500,001 to $1,000,000$600,001 to $1,200,000
6.50%Over $1,000,000Over $1,200,000

Local income tax is the second layer. Counties may charge up to 3.30% for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. Harford County lists 3.06% and Howard County 3.20% for calendar 2026.

Because a house gain is counted in income, a large gain can push the year's income into a higher bracket. A tax professional can run the numbers for your own return.

How does the federal home sale exclusion work for a Maryland seller?

Under IRS Topic 701, you can exclude up to $250,000 of gain from the sale of your main home, or $500,000 if you file jointly. To qualify you must have owned the home at least 24 months and lived in it as your main home at least 24 months during the 5 years ending on the sale date.

The two tests can be met in different 2-year periods. You generally cannot take the exclusion if you excluded gain from another home sale in the 2 years before this one.

A reduced exclusion may be available when the sale is driven by a work, health or unforeseeable event, such as a death, divorce or a home destroyed by disaster. The IRS formula divides your qualifying time by 730 days and multiplies by $250,000. Report the sale if you receive Form 1099-S or if you cannot exclude all of the gain, using Schedule D and Form 8949.

What federal rates apply when the gain is more than the exclusion?

Gain on a home owned more than one year is taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% federally, depending on income. The IRS lists these ceilings for tax years beginning in 2025:

  • 0% up to $48,350 for single filers, $96,700 for joint filers and $64,750 for heads of household.
  • 15% above that, up to $533,400 for single filers, $600,050 for joint filers and $566,700 for heads of household.
  • 20% above the 15% range.

Gain on a home held one year or less is short-term and taxed as ordinary income. Unrecaptured section 1250 gain from real property, which comes from depreciation, is taxed at up to 25%.

The 3.8% net investment income tax can also apply. Its thresholds are $200,000 for single filers and heads of household and $250,000 for joint filers. Gain on a principal residence generally escapes it to the extent the gain is excluded, while gain above the exclusion can count.

How do you work out the gain on a Maryland house?

The gain is the amount realized minus your adjusted basis. The IRS defines amount realized as the selling price minus selling expenses, and basis starts with what you paid, including purchase costs, then rises with improvements that add value.

Because selling expenses reduce the amount realized, the closing costs you pay at settlement come back into the math. Keep the final settlement statement.

Inherited houses follow a special rule. Your basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death, or the alternate valuation date the estate chose. If an estate tax return was filed or required, the value on that return is your basis.

Rental or business use needs care. The IRS says depreciation claimed after May 6, 1997 cannot be excluded and is recognized as unrecaptured section 1250 gain. Periods after 2008 when the property was not your principal residence are generally nonqualified use, and gain allocated to those periods cannot be excluded.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maryland houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What does a nonresident seller of Maryland real estate owe at closing?

A nonresident selling Maryland real property must have tax withheld at settlement: 8.75% of the total payment for individuals and 8.25% for entities, for sales after June 30, 2025. The deed cannot be recorded unless the withholding payment accompanies it.

Form MW506NRS reports it. Sellers who owe less, or none, can apply for an early refund when the sale price is below $1.5 million. At $1.5 million or more, no tentative refund is available and the seller files a full annual return, with Form 502CG where it applies. Form MW506AE is the application for a certificate of full or partial exemption.

The withholding does not include the extra 2% surtax. A seller who expects that tax should make additional estimated payments, using Form 502D.

Seller typeWithholding on sales after June 30, 2025
Nonresident individual8.75% of total payment
Nonresident entity8.25% of total payment

Do Maryland taxes change if the buyer pays cash or is an investor?

No. Maryland and federal tax on your gain follow your basis, your holding period and your income, not who buys the house or how the buyer pays. A cash buyer simply means the price you realize is the price in the contract.

What a quick cash sale changes is time. If you want to qualify for the home sale exclusion, check the 24-month tests before you sign, because the date of sale is the date that counts.

Keep the settlement statement, the closing disclosure from your purchase and receipts for improvements. Those documents prove your basis if the IRS or the Comptroller asks.

More questions about Maryland Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Is there a Maryland capital gains tax on selling a home?

Maryland taxes the gain as income, with local tax on top, and adds a 2% surtax on net capital gains when federal adjusted gross income is above $350,000. A primary residence that sells for less than $1.5 million is excluded from that surtax.

How much of my home sale gain can I exclude federally?

Up to $250,000 if you file as single, or $500,000 for joint filers. You must have owned the home and used it as your main home for at least 24 months in the 5 years before the sale.

Do Maryland counties add tax to my capital gain?

Yes, through the local income tax, which is capped at 3.30% for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. Harford County lists 3.06% and Howard County 3.20%.

What happens if I live out of state and sell a Maryland house?

Tax is withheld at settlement: 8.75% for a nonresident individual and 8.25% for an entity. You can apply for a refund of the excess if the price is below $1.5 million, and above that you file a full annual return.

What is my tax basis in an inherited Maryland house?

It is generally the fair market value on the date of death, or the alternate valuation date the estate chose. If an estate tax return was required or filed, the value on it is your basis.
